data.hypothesis: A factor-two target mapping with 128 threads per block and 256 outputs per block may retain source-register reuse while lowering per-CTA register allocation relative to the previously measured 256-thread factor-two configuration. The occupancy and scheduling effect is hardware-dependent and must be measured; no speedup is assumed.

memory_lessons.applicability: These measurements concern the same target-axis coarsening path, but they do not establish why the candidates were slower.
memory_lessons.claim: The measured factor-four candidate was correct but slower than baseline (0.004442 s versus 0.001847 s). The measured factor-two candidate was also correct and slower than baseline (0.002727 s), while faster than the factor-four candidate. Lower coarsening is a useful experiment, not proof of a win.
memory_lessons.next_experiment: Measure the 128-thread, 256-output factor-two configuration using the full correctness suite and official timing metric.

data.notes: The supplied current source is the baseline, so this candidate introduces the factor-two mapping directly. It bounds-checks both targets for arbitrary N, preserves each target's source-loop accumulation order and input mass, and uses no shared-memory staging. Register use, occupancy, correctness, and official timing remain for the controller to evaluate.
transformations: Assign two output particles to each thread using target indices separated by blockDim.x; use 128 threads and 256 logical outputs per block.
Load each streamed source particle's position and mass once per source-loop iteration and reuse them across both valid targets with separate force accumulators.
Bounds-check each target, skip only its own self-interaction, and write each valid output once; retain shared_memory_bytes at zero.
